en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Haiyin from the Three Assemblies.
In the summer of the Great Zhi (Wu-shen) year, Xun-shen held an *Ullambana* feast for his late mother, Lady Ding, and invited Chan Master Haiyin of Huili Temple to expound the Dharma.
Thereupon, I had the opportunity to attend upon Master Wansong, and we engaged in deep conversation for several days. The Master was greatly...
Regarding his capacity as a vessel: it was said that during his previous lives, he had come and gone with ease;

whenever I raised a point for him to explain, he would simply smile and say, "I thought the old monk had something special. From then on, we were deeply in accord. The following year, I traveled north, while the Master went to reside at Jianfu Temple in Jiangdong.
When I returned to the mountain, the Master also retired to rest at Baolin Temple. While he was afflicted by illness, he sent a monk to deliver this message.
He wrote a verse by hand, ending with: "The wondrous turning of the pivot was previously understood; the moon over the eastern eaves illuminates past and present.

This refers to how the Master once praised the portrait of his late father, the District Prefect of Wucheng, saying: "Throughout heaven and earth, ancient and today, the moon shines upon the eastern eaves.
On the day his father passed away, the Master wrote a eulogy which said: "Traversing on the wind, the autumn moon hangs in the midst of heaven. Such was the Master’s intent.
The meaning of [the title] "In the Third" is identical from ancient times to the present. Reflecting upon this boundless debt of gratitude, tears fall in profusion.
Formerly, when Dahuì requested an inscription for the stupa of Zhantang, Wújìn Jūshì received the inquiry:
"The eye does not perish... and he subsequently said: "This vajra... [text fragment].
My teacher is the present-day Zhantang. As for his diamond-eye, it has long been [shining].
His *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) was compiled by his disciple Xingchun. He intends to carve it into woodblocks for wide distribution and has sent a messenger to my residence to seek a preface.
Although I am truly unable to contribute a single word, the bond of friendship leaves me with no choice but to comply.
Alas! The primary meaning (paramārtha) is beyond verbal expression; how could it be understood through the cognition of the intellect, or through deliberation and discrimination?
The Master’s Way is like water following the shape of its vessel.

If one says, "This water is square, round, curved, straight, large, or small," these differences belong to the vessels themselves; it is not that the water itself possesses duality. Behold this record.

This is because one must not restrict their capacity; otherwise, in the final five hundred years, it would be like pouring ocean into ocean, or else one will become entangled in a self-woven tangle, like trying to untie something while drenched in lacquer.
Preface by Zeng Xunshen, Compiler at the Hanlin Academy and Court Historian’s Bureau,
on the *Recorded Sayings of Master Haiyin*, dated the [blank] day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Yanyou era.
Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of the Chan Monasteries of Muping and Xinghua in Yuanzhou.
Recorded Sayings of Huili Chan Temple on Ruiyun Mountain at Linjiang;
Recorded Sayings of Jian Chan Temple in Donghu, Raozhou;
Verses on Ancient Cases (Gong'an); Eulogies for Buddhas and Patriarchs; Self-Portraits and Eulogies.
Postscript to the Inscription for the Stupa;
Recorded Sayings of Venerable Haiyin while Residing at Xinghua Chan Temple on Mount Muping in Yuanzhou.

The disciple Xingchun compiled [this record] on the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year of the Zhizhen era. At that time, the Master was at the Head Seat’s Quarters on Mount Yang, having accepted an invitation.
He entered the temple and, pointing to the Dharma seat, said:

"The place where the Buddhas of the three periods have not reached, and where the old monks of the world have not been able to speak—it is here that New Muping shall now present it all at once to everyone. With a sudden stride, he ascended the seat.
Having finished the prayers for the Emperor, he again held up incense and said:
"I respectfully offer this for my current abbot at Dayang Mountain, the Great Zen Master Huilang, the Venerable Xueyan, to repay the kindness of his Dharma-milk. Thereupon, he adjusted his robes.
[The Master] takes his seat. A monk asks: "The Buddhas of the three periods have not reached it; the old monks of the world have not spoken of it.
Before this Dharma-seat of gods and humans, I beg the Master to speak one clear phrase. [The Master] [responds]. [The assembly] prays for the longevity of the Emperor.
The ocean-like multitude has all arrived. The student comes forward and requests the Master to [bestow]... [the Master]... [bestows].
[The Master] said: "The mountains and rivers are majestic; the imperial residence is grand. The student asked:
"I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the prayers for the Emperor. As for the matter of the supreme vehicle (zōngchéng) that transcends this, what is it?

The Master said: "This is far removed from [ordinary] speech. The student asked: "If so, then every word reveals the ultimate truth, and every sentence points toward the source. The Master said: "That too is [merely conventional]."
This is for everyday use. [The student] advances and says: "Let us set this matter aside for a moment. It is just like when the Great Zen Buddha arrived at Mount Yangshang;
he circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his mendicant’s staff once, and stood on one foot, saying: 'The four or seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven were like this;
the two or three patriarchs of the Tang land were like this; the old monks of all under heaven were like this; and you, Master, are also like this.'"
[The monk] said, "So-and-so. I am also like this. Yangshan struck him with four blows of the rattan staff.

What was the meaning of this? The Master said, "It divided Mount Tai and Mount Hua; it split the Yellow River asunder. [The monk] further asked, "As for 'Great Chan Buddha,' later when he reached Huoshan, Huoshan said, 'Under Jiyun Peak, four blows of the rattan staff.
Great Chan Buddha from all under heaven, come forward! Huoshan then called for the rector to strike the bell. Great Chan Buddha—"
[The monk] ran off. [The Master asked: "And what about that? The Master said, "The thief is a petty person, yet his wit surpasses that of a gentleman.
The monk pressed further: "Later Xuedou said, 'The rattan staff has not yet reached the point of breaking. Why did he only strike four times? Furthermore, how is this?
The Master said, "Eight taels on the left, seven taels on the right. The monk said, "As for you, Master, who personally saw Yangshan—tell me, how does this compare?"
"How far apart are Mahācīna and the Buddha? The Master said, "I am a man from Xingan.
The monk said, "If that is so, then there has been no difference between past and present; it is clearly right before our eyes. The Master said, "It is very far away. The monk bowed.
The Master then said, "This seal of the Dharma of mine is spoken for the sake of benefiting the world. Guard this secret treasury with care; do not treat it lightly."
The proclamation: Today the seams of the brocade are flung wide open, and its patterns are fully revealed. Sentient and insentient beings alike are sealed by a single seal.
It is such that even Stonehead Buddha has no way to evade it, and Mount Bowel-Pot Peak cannot contain it.
At this very moment, have you yet grasped the matter of transcending the world? After a long silence, he said: "Still holding the golden whip, I ask the traveler returning home."
"Who walks the Imperial Street with me at nightfall?
Jǔ, the founding Chan Master Dàoshān, first visited Master Luǒpǔ and asked: "Before a single bubble has arisen, how can one discern the course of the water?
Luǒpǔ replied: "Shift the boat to understand the currents; lift the oars to distinguish the waves. Dàoshān did not find this satisfactory. Later...
Chan Master Paramen returned to the previous question. Wen said, "If you move your boat, you do not part from the water;

yet as soon as you raise your oars, you lose the source. Dao attained great enlightenment on the spot. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "Although these two elders possessed the eyes to distinguish dragons from snakes and capture tigers and rhinoceroses, they could not avoid mixing mud with water.
For Chan Master Dao to attain enlightenment in such a manner was also to remain within the mud."
Washing away the clods of earth; Xingmuping examines things in this manner. Is there still any trace of the ancients’ insight?
If the great ocean were to know contentment, the hundred rivers would surely flow backward.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Before a single bubble has arisen, the earth is vast and the heavens are wide. Mountain clouds drift slowly; mountain stream waters murmur. To see Muping here is easy;
to see Zhenji is difficult. Why? Because the south of Jiangnan has warm earth, while the north of the Great Wall has cold skies."
The two orders remain for the ascent to the hall. Neither old nor new, neither advancing nor retreating—Heaven covers because of this, and Earth bears because of this.
Nevertheless, even the sovereigns Yao and Shun still had their transformative influence remaining.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I recall that in the past, a monk asked the founding Master, 'What is the meaning of Muping?
He replied, 'No need for axe or hatchet. What was the intent of this? The Master said, "A master hand’s work is difficult to replicate. The monk pressed further:
"That monk then asked again, 'What is the meaning of "no need for axe or hatchet"? He replied, 'Muping. How about that? The Master said, "It is still..."
"There is still a sharp edge remaining. The monk prostrated. The Master then said, "The Dharma King who shatters existence has appeared in the world.
He suddenly took up his staff; the staff is existence. He struck once and said, "Right now it is shattered. Do you see the Dharma King appearing?"
Relying on the Master, he kills all people under heaven with his doubt.
Ascending the hall, [he said: (In gratitude to the Abbot Guangnan Hai). A bright pearl in the vast sea; its light illuminates the universe. Mazu gazing at the moon.
Nanquan brushed aside his sleeves. But as for the saying, "The sutras return to the Canon; Chan returns to the Sea"—how is this so? A single imperial post road:
from ancient times until now, there have been those who have traveled it.

Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: For six years in the Snowy Mountains, he wore clothes that bared his elbows; at midnight, beneath the morning star, he pointed to a locust tree and called it a willow.
To then say, "The wisdom and virtuous marks of the Tathāgata are possessed by all sentient beings throughout the earth," is merely to air one's own family’s dirty laundry.
It is only fitting. Yunmen’s single blow was intended to kill the dog; "Mute!"—those who forget their debt are many, while those who recognize it are few.
Upon returning from the city, he ascended the hall and said: "This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true. In the empty mountains, amidst the white clouds, there is clamor.
The marketplace is a sea of red dust; heaven is high and boundless, earth is vast and without limit. The radish from Zhenzhou weighs three catties.

Ascending the hall: February has passed, March arrives; a thousand shades of red and ten thousand hues of purple are washed by the rain and withered by the wind. In a fleeting glance, one beholds the empty mountain.
On a clear day, amidst the shadows of green willows, a single tree of white peach blossoms opens. Before the wind, she stands still, lingering for a moment.
Hehehe! No one knows this meaning; alone she ascends the high terrace.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: “The Zen of the Tathāgata, the intent of the Patriarchs—when the rooster is cold it climbs the tree;
when the duck is cold it enters the water. It is so, and yet it is not so. It is not so, and yet it is not not-so.
If you all gain a sudden flash of insight here, only then will you know: having removed the nostrils, with what will you sneeze?”

Ascending the hall, he said: "Zen is neither sitting nor reclining; it is also free from effort and achievement. The Way has nothing to be grasped or rejected; it completely transcends seeing and hearing.
What need is there to speak of the 'pine tree,' the 'dry dung pellet,' or the 'three pounds of flax'? The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have swallowed them all in one gulp.
Truly so! One hears the words, but does not see the person."

Ascending the hall to pray for rain: "In the scorching heat of the sixth month, the rain has still not fallen. He raises his staff and strikes it once, saying: "He lashes forth the dragon from the azure depths;
let there be three days of rain, so that the seasons may be harmonious and the harvests abundant. *Du!* (A shout).
Ascending the hall on the first day of the seventh month, [the Master] said: "A different melody when the strings are moved. He struck once with his whisk. "Do you hear it?
"The leaves falling let one know autumn. He swept once with the whisk. "Do you see it?
"Even if you were beyond hearing and seeing, beyond what is seen and heard, you would still be separated from the green mountains by several points of cloud."

Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the retreat: The wild goose and the snow are white throughout their entire bodies; The man of winter is his whole being ice. Dejectedly, he has no skillful means;
Directly beneath him, all achievement and merit are severed. In the whistling autumn wind, leaning on a thin cane, he gazes quietly: On the south and north of the mountain, cold clouds arise.
Ascending the hall: Within the realm of seeing and hearing, amidst movement and stillness, it is inexhaustible when sought and infinite in its application.
At midday, the sun blazes fiercely; at night deep, the cool wind rustles. From the bamboo fence to the corners of the walls, one gradually hears the chirping and buzzing of autumn insects.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Master Baiyun Wenzhun. When he first visited Master Yangqi Fanghui, Fanghui asked him, "I have heard that your teacher has a verse on the realization of the Way;
try reciting it for me. Baiyun then recited: "I possess a divine pearl, Long locked away by the dust of worldly toil.
Today the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers. Thereupon, Yangqi was greatly...
Xiao Baiyun harbored doubts and did not sleep all night. The following day, he entered the room to inquire about them. It was then the end of the year;
Huaihui said, "Did you see the one who struck the night-fox yesterday? He replied, "I saw him. Huaihui said, "In this matter, you fall short of him by one move."
He loves being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. Under these words, Baiyun attained great enlightenment. The Master commented:
"Master Yu picked up a single pea and called it a bright pearl. This drew Baiyun to cherish it as a supreme treasure.
It did not take Yangqi’s light touch to break through this; it was not worth a single coin. In the beginning, he could not help but leave the people of the world in doubt. Later...
His face smiles so as to kill all the people under heaven. When one examines this closely, it is truly laughable. Why?
It is still possible to take earth and turn it into gold; however, to transform gold back into earth is indeed difficult.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit?
To ask such a question is easy; to maintain its continuity is very difficult. Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes?
Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. Great Kāśyapa, elder brother as he was, was brought directly to his end by Ānanda’s single question.
The score was not settled. Later, Master Fenyang said: "Without asking, how can one know? For now, do not pretend to be clear-headed.
Master Wuzu Jie said: "Exposed error. Master Cuoyan Zhi said: "A thousand-year-old tree without a shadow."
"Nowadays, people wear bottomless boots; they look for holes to wedge in [nails]. What use is there in that? Master Letan Qing said:
"Before the banner-pole has fallen, I have already pierced the nostrils of you all and replaced your eyes.
After the banner-pole has fallen, where will you see Old Śākyamuni? *Zha!*" Master Xingkong Guan said: "What kind of talk is this?"
Talk. Now, I ask you all: would you be able to overturn the banner-pole at the gate? Would that suffice for the purport of the "separate transmission outside the teachings"?
Hanging up the head of a sheep while selling dog meat—although these great elders uphold the very marrow of the higher path, they cannot avoid giving rise to interpretations based on words.
Wood Flat (Muping) had no special talent, yet he too wished to bring the ancients back to life.
"One eye. Suddenly he took up his staff and struck it once, leaving the people of the world in doubt.
This is the *Recorded Sayings* of Venerable Haiyin of Huili Chan Temple on Mount Ruiyun by the River Linjiang;
compiled by his disciple Daozhang.
Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday. A monk asked, "I recall the Emperor Taizong asking a monk, 'Where have you recently come from?

The monk replied, 'From Amidst the Clouds. Taizong said, 'If you are deep within the clouds, you do not pay court to the Emperor. Why then have you arrived here? The monk was speechless. "What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Heaven and earth cannot contain it; the universe does not know its name. The monk stepped forward and asked further.
Later, Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying: "It is difficult to escape the ultimate transformation. [The student] asked: "And what about this? The Master said:
"Though gold dust is precious, falling into the eye becomes a cataract. [The student] further asked: "What about right now?"
[On] the Imperial Birthday of the Heavenly Longevity, [a monk] asked, "I do not know how the Master intends to offer his congratulations.

The Master said, "The entire nation knows well. The monk stepped forward and said, "When the dragon meets the water, its spirit increases; when the tiger encounters the mountain scenery, its fierce majesty grows.

The Master said, "From a high place, one observes that even the lofty is insufficient. The monk bowed. The Master then said: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Ruler..."
If the king attains this One, the world will be greatly governed. But tell me: from where does this One arise? [He] strikes the meditation staff:
"How great is the Qian-primordial! All things receive their beginning from it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree. When the tree falls, the vine withers.
Why then have you come from three thousand miles away, selling your cotton robe? Put down your clay bowl! Ha ha ha! Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago;
yet until this very day, the wondrous truth has not been attained."

Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, he had already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings was already complete.
Does Old Śākyamuni have any place of appearing or disappearing? A foul reputation and a tainted trace are difficult to wash clean. Yunmen’s command does not fail to take effect.
After descending from the seat, proceed to the Buddha Hall for the general invitation and perform three prostrations of great respect; grant them all this at once.

Having covered [the hall] and retired, he held a small *sīmā-bandha* (retreat) *śamaya*. To protect life, one must kill; only when killing is exhausted does one dwell in peace. This is the livelihood within the ghost cave.
If you can grasp the meaning herein, even the floating of an iron boat upon the water is merely a forced explanation of principle. Under Master Ruijun’s gate—[one].

Letting dragons and snakes mingle, and ordinary beings and sages intersect—making no distinction between insects, plants, and trees, or sentient and insentient beings—all enter together into the pure ocean of awakening.
They swim in the wisdom of equality: those who eat, eat; those who doze, doze.
(He strikes the staff. In this world of peace and clarity, there is not a single idle spot.
The next day, he ascended the hall. Ruiyun’s "One Barrier" seems casual; it is easy to speak of, yet difficult to penetrate.
The green ivy winds its way up to the very summit of the cold pine; the white clouds drift lightly, appearing and disappearing within the vast void.
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. Suppose there were a man who did not observe the sacred regulations and did not dwell in a monastery—how would you instruct him?
He planted his staff in the ground and gave a shout.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Take one step forward—ten-thousand-fathom silver mountains. Take one step back—a thousand-fathom iron walls.
At such a time as this, if you all know the phrase for turning around, you will see the moon over the clear river, vast and fully manifest;
you will hear the wind in the great pines, ceaselessly and eternally speaking. After a long silence, he added: "Great or small Ruijun, you have split the talk into two separate pieces."

Ascending the hall: It has been over half a month since the summer retreat began. How can that matter be explained? The Cold Mountain Man, the Water Ox, the wax figure, and the ice goose guarding the snow—all these are merely boring through the void in search of a hollow.
In other quarters, it is difficult to see but easy to recognize; here at Ruijun, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize.
Even if you were to bring all conditions to rest and not leave behind a single word, should you hesitate for even a moment, there will be a thunderclap from the blue sky.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When questioned, they do not know; when pressed, they do not understand. The ultimate principle and the profound pivot are but lumps of clay and clods of earth.
Whether you know or not, whether you understand or not—where the white clouds end, there is the green mountain; the traveler stands even beyond the green mountain."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: After the Patriarch Huineng had attained the Dharma but before he had shaved his head, he was staying at Faxing Temple in Guangzhou.
At that time, the wind blew the temple banner. One monk said, "The wind moves. Another monk said, "The banner moves. They argued back and forth without end.
The Patriarch asked, "May a layman like me presume to join this noble discussion? The monks replied, "You may do so. The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving."
"Movement! The mind of the benevolent one moves. The two monks ceased their dispute.
Today, when I, this unworthy descendant, examine the matter, although Patriarch Lu was able to settle the dispute between the two monks, he could not, after all, make the two monks truly alive.
If it were Ruiyun, however, it would be otherwise. Taking up his staff, he showed it to the assembly and said: "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. Nor is it..."
This mind moves; he throws down his staff and asks, "What is this?

He ascends the hall for the assembly on the occasion of the *Sānqīngmiáo jīng* (Sutra of the Green Sprouts). To explain the meaning by relying on the sutra is to be an enemy of the Buddhas of the three periods;
to deviate from a single word of the sutra is to speak like a demon. It is just as when Master Guishan asked Master Yangshan, "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, how much is..."

The Buddha said: "How much of this is the Buddha's teaching and how much is Māra's teaching? Yangshan replied: "It is all Māra's teaching. When one reaches this point, how can one distinguish between them?
It is like placing snow in a silver bowl; do not speak of it before those without wisdom, lest you strike their heads until they split and their brains spill out.
Addressing the assembly: Keep the body upright; keep the posture straight. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, maintain a single-pointed focus on the word "Mu.

Exert yourself with fierce diligence, like a lone man facing ten thousand enemies. Let go of all emotions until breath is forgotten. Be cool and still, empty and silent. Three great kalpas are but a single thought;
the four great oceans are but a single drop. There is no trace of dullness or distraction. Buddhas and patriarchs—rest!
Seeking and investigating: movement and stillness settle heaven and earth; illumination and function thunder like a clap of lightning. If you can act thus, your studies are complete.
Originally, your own self is a wall of cast iron. A wall of iron, a wall of iron!
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Sweat flows without end; waving the fan does not bring relief.

Suddenly striking upon a leopard-footed flower-patterned mosquito, one attains a state of total, smooth ease, such that joy knows no bounds. Therefore it is said: 'Only when all are slain does one dwell in peace.
Do you all perceive this or not? When a mute man has a dream, to whom can he tell it? A wooden man laughs until his lips split. If you understand it thus..."

Depart! You are truly a master of the Way. Had you not yet gone to the quarters to offer thanks, you would have missed the opportunity. Descending from the seat, he circulates through the hall for tea. Regarding the Small Assembly for the End of the Retreat:
In these ninety days of restraining the feet, the fish has cast itself into the net; though it is a scaled dragon that surges through the waves, it still lags within the water.

During these three months of summer retreat, the bird has entered its cage; though it is a majestic wing that soars to the heavens, it remains lost amidst the clouds. When life and death are both exhausted, the silkworm makes its cocoon; as soon as...
As soon as there is something held as weighty, one creates a nest of habitual patterns. How can one penetrate these three layers? To speak of "three layers" is already too much;

there are hundreds of turns and thousands of folds—all must be penetrated at once. Test the wax man to see whether he is frozen or not; pity the goose that guards the snow, yet does not let it become snow.
These are always matters of daily life. Now that the three periods have reached their completion, the myriad practices are spontaneously perfected.
Having arrived at this point, do you all know how to distinguish the timing and what is appropriate for the occasion? When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the whole world;
the water’s luster and clouds’ shadows drift on a vast sky. (He sets down his staff. Who will come forward to take up the hook that defies destiny?
Master Dongshan Kong addressed the assembly, saying: "A hundred-fold refined gold is cast into an iron ox;
it is offered to others at its full value. Before the courtyard, there are no flowers smiling; this too is Dongshan’s rest for the summer. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "..."
Master Kong spoke thus: "It is much like buying cheap in the east and selling dear in the west; wanting to add where there is too much and subtract where there is too little.
One cannot avoid the price failing to reach its mark or the negotiation remaining incomplete. This summer at Ruijun, I have laid it all out as best I can:
Hanshanzi, the water buffalo, the wax man, the icicle, and the iron pellet—these I share with you all from the same bowl."

Rice. He does not treat it as base, nor does he treat it as noble. When traveling east, he does not look for profit while traveling west. Whether there is profit or no profit, he does not fail to frequent the marketplace.
Ruijun is simply handing it over to others; yet there is nothing to be sought. Silence! To see it and not take it, one must think of it from a thousand miles away.
The next day he ascended the hall and untied the mouth of his cloth bag: "The paths to the south and north are open; the ten directions have no walls.
In the three realms, all traces of movement cease. To the west is the west, and to the east is the east; the wandering clouds and waters naturally layer upon one another."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Walk with confidence in your feet; speak with confidence in your mouth. In its application, there is no need for fabrication. Suddenly treading upon Fu-ma Bridge, one unconsciously strikes through the broken stove.
Just so—and yet not just so—one recalls the words Guizong once spoke: 'The head-dhuta rock is enveloped by moss.'* Striking his whisk against the meditation seat, he descended. *Note:

This refers to the famous encounter between Guizong and the monk Daowu, where the rock symbolizes the unconditioned nature of reality. The "moss" represents the habitual tendencies that obscure it. The master’s action with the whisk signifies the sudden breakthrough of realization.*
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ape carries its young back behind the green peaks; the bird picks up falling flowers before the azure cliffs.

For twenty years, people have understood this only as a description of external scenery, thereby obscuring the mechanism of the trap with brocade. He then asked: "If you do not understand it as a description of scenery, after all, how do you understand it?"

An iron-wrapped lump of mud; its name cannot be translated between Chinese and Sanskrit. To call for a response, there must be a source. At the gate of Ruiyun, not even a hair’s breadth can be deceived. Why?
Though we lean together upon the same balustrade, we do not view the mountain colors in the same way.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "In the past, a monk asked Touzi, 'When a person who has undergone the great death comes back to life, what then?
Touzi replied, 'Night travel is not permitted; one must arrive by dawn. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "From Southern Heaven to the Five Terraces of the North.
The monk further asked: "I do not understand, Master. The Master said: "Three thousand blows by day; eight hundred blows by night. The monk bowed.

[The student] bows. The Master then said: "The emergence of words and traces is the source from which divergent paths arise. Before words had emerged and before traces had taken form, there was no internal and no external;
there was no 'that' and no 'this'; there was no distant and no near. There was not a single thread of hair that was not already manifest and complete.

Yet when it comes to being internal and external simultaneously, being 'that' and 'this' simultaneously, being distant and near simultaneously—then they flourish profusely and transform wondrously, leaving no lingering attachment."
At such a time as this, how can one communicate? Heaven and earth cannot contain it; from antiquity to the present, its name has remained unknown.

Entering the hall, he said: "It seems to exist and yet seems not to; it is half real and half false. It leaves the people of the world in doubt; it does not lie within the realm of 'it' (zhi), 'this' (hu), or 'that' (zhe)."
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you must know where you yourself truly stand. If you do know, then pass your time with coarse gruel and plain rice.

you have already traveled extensively through the gateways of the various elders. "Green surpasses blue; bluer than blue. You stand as a model for the many scholars, crowning the East.
Southward, guest and host converse clearly; long and short verses allow one to explore the profound mystery. Wherever the staff and cane reach, it is like the appearance of the udumbara flower.

The night moon is exquisite, the pines rustle softly; I deeply hope that our slender shadows may share this moss-covered grotto. One’s power of concentration is already firm, making even the Vairambha wind seem light.
Deshan and Linji would have been left speechless in their silence.
To Master Fang I show: Ten thousand miles, not a blade of grass; the sun shines brightly across the heavens. To step out the door is already treading on grass;

reaching the ground is the Chang’an road. No one stands at the edge of the courtyard; even the traces of the ancient path have been swept away. Entrusting this to you, Master Fang, go ask the void for an answer.
Xiaoshan Gufeng held forth on the seasonal themes of pines and plum blossoms as he visited me with a handscroll.
I inscribe this after him: After the snow, Gufeng returned to Xiaoguan; I came to Ruijun and traveled back and forth. How many pairs of sandals can one wear before gazing upon the green mountains?

Unfolding the plum scroll, we both share a smile—our faces are equally weathered by age. The pact between the man of Mount Gu and the man of Mount Shan remains unbroken; Chan-escaping, the spirit of Chan is captured in ink.
Not yet dry. The left-hand official Ji Xiao bears a weight of ten thousand *qun*. The guests sit in awe, entrusting him with the task of explaining its difficulty.

Creation has no beginning; it lies within the span of unfolding and rolling up. To be the spring before all under heaven is no ordinary matter. When the year ends, we shall look upon one another as two elders.
This poem and this painting are treasures of both ancient and modern times.
The Layman Ziran of Piling is neither cause nor condition, yet not non-natural. He is spontaneously so, yet both so and not so. There is no "so" that is not self-natured;
there is no self-nature that is not so. That which is not so is eternally manifest before us. These words perfectly accord with the Way.
The earth comes first; from it, the myriad transformations emerge vast and boundless. In this majestic daily life, by whose power does one ride?
To Shi Youzhou’s attendant, Ciyun Yu:
the stones are rugged and the jade is brilliant. Its radiance is perfectly round; dust and mud naturally dissolve into grit. It is neither carved nor chiseled.
Polishing and refining it, one laughs instead at Cao Shan for exposing his sharp edges; the student who seeks a teacher merely carries a raw gem in vain.
"Jade! Jade! Do you know it or not? When the old rustic calls out three times, who responds? Only by breaking it open does one realize it is one's own;
its value exceeds that of ten cities, so do not offer it lightly. It naturally possesses a radiance that fills the entire universe.

The Buddhas and Patriarchs praised the wisdom and virtuous marks of leaving the mountain; who on this great earth does not possess them? To claim awakening upon seeing the stars is but a hollow pretension that has spread its poison to the present day.
Not yet finished. Heretical teachings are difficult to support.

[The inscription for a portrait of Avalokiteśvara by Li Jichuan, Administrative Judge of Gan Prefecture, whose family had long resided in Rao: "Formerly, there was a silk painting of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) that was cast adrift by the winds and waters. The Bodhisattva acts as a fisherman, wielding the net of the True Dharma to enter the sea of birth and death, gathering in sentient beings and leading them to the shore of Great Enlightenment.
In the past, within the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate, I have often recited its words; now, regarding the painted image of Avalokiteśvara in the Water obtained from Master Jichuan, the matter is verified.
Thus we know that the power of the Dharma manifests through transformation, and both word and image are truly real. There must certainly be...
Entering the ocean of the pure mind and attaining indestructible faith is self-evident. The verse says:
Unfurling and rolling up, it circulates through all time; Most difficult to digest is this heart of great compassion. The whole body enters the water, the whole body emerges;
Yet alas, the ocean of karma of those sentient beings is deep.
A fisherman’s basket holds scales of brocade; dewdrops form a necklace. Though years have passed like this, his lofty character remains free from worldly dust.
The basket still has eyes—how could it ever deceive anyone?
Master Yushan picked up a bright pearl;
he valued it as little as donkey dung. The stream bridge lies submerged in the waters of Mischuan;
it is precisely the yellow ox.
A single word is not settled; riding an ox while searching for the ox. Ten thousand layers of Cold Mountain’s emerald green flow like a stream.
At sunrise, waiting for the moon, the heavens and sea are high;
the mountain moon is small. The great earth is a scroll of scripture—when will it ever be finished reading? Let go of your own self.
Dawn. A needle with a pierced nose, without thread. One bite and it is severed; it naturally forms a piece. The bright sun appears in the midst of the sky.
Bodhidharma.

Failing to reach accord with King Liang, he ceased speaking of there being no one in the eastern lands; yet by ordering the Second Patriarch to seek the mind, he acted as if there were a Buddha in the Western Heavens.
The moon grows cold at Shaolin; the Yangtze River is empty. To this day, the snowy waves cry out in the frosty wind.

Since Zhenzan was established as head seat, his conduct has been such that he never steps ahead of others, nor does he fall behind them. In his later years, he moved to Donghu; though his speech became sparse, his Way grew ever more profound.
Unless it were otherwise, it could not be clarified by brush or ink. Entrust this to the Head Seat Xuecen:
look at what kind of face this is! Oṃ phaṭ chiṭ chuṭ śodhaya.
Requested by Huang Ao Dunweng.
The great raw jade remains uncarved; there is no chiseling or polishing. Essence and spirit are gathered and unified; the point is concealed and the edge withdrawn.

Returning to the midst of worldly toil, though one traverses myriad conditions, the ancestral teachers' pivot is fully upheld—a single move prior to the mechanism. In ordinary practice, one uses only the blunt tongs and hammer, leaving it for all people of the world to attempt to sketch and describe.

Master Chuchu of Jing’an abides in stillness and single-mindedness. A smiling face meets a wrathful fist; he is gentle yet stern. He offends others by disregarding taboos, saying, "This is one and two," or "If this is not it, then who else could it be?
Beyond the bamboo, the distant mountains are as green as eyebrows.
A Postscript to the Letter of Master Fozhao, Requested by Elder Nangang.
When Master Fozhao was at Lingjing, Master Yi was presiding over the state; with the protection of the sovereign and his ministers from without, he was able to practice his Way. Consequently...
There were elder masters such as Guyun Xiu and Yankong Sǒu who appeared one after another; one can thus imagine the flourishing state of the Dharma community at that time.
It happened that while holding my alms bowl, I came to Jiwén and visited Nángāng at Longhuá. He brought forth this scroll and showed it to me;
I lit incense and contemplated its meaning, feeling a deep sense of poignant sorrow for a long time.
The Calligraphy of Chijue on the "Eulogy of Boyi":
The lofty wind of Boyi and Shuqi is as vast as heaven and earth and spans ten thousand generations. Su Shi praised it; Wen Tianxiang eulogized it; now the Elder Chijue [does so as well].
Jiefangyan wrote this in small clerical script. Although we are far apart in distance, our mutual esteem is the same. Where the Way is shared, the principle is in accord, and thus we are neighbors.
Among us, Chijue was still slightly superior. Why? Because within the royal treasury, there is no such blade as that.
Regarding Mingji Xitang: During his southern tour to examine his own practice, he requested a colophon for this work.
In the auspicious month of the Great Yiyou year, while the slight chill lingered after the sun had warmed the day, I was leaning against a table at my "Pine and Bamboo" retreat.
Just then, there was the sound of a knocker; opening the door to look, it was Mingji Xitang, holding in his hand [a record of] his southern tour to examine himself.
He had already completed one fascicle of his own work and said to me, "The various great elders have already written much; I request that Haiyin provide a few words.
I then accepted it and unfolded it, reading through it thoroughly and repeatedly to examine the realms where Mingji had traveled and the landscapes he had beheld.

Everything was vividly present within the mind. Looking on until suddenly a fine wind arose and shook the earth, he rode upon that wind to observe the three thousand great thousandfold worlds and all realms as numerous as motes of dust.
He entered the samādhi of dozing; unconsciously, his breathing became like thunder.
When it grew intensely bright, [the master] shook him and recited the final phrase. Thereupon, he rubbed his sleepy eyes, rolled up [his vision], and returned to it, saying: "The same."
Each person dreams on their own bed; only those who share the same awakening can know it.
Thus spoke the Dharma to the attendant Mingliao.

Vividly clear at the tips of the hundred grasses, vividly clear is the meaning of the Patriarchs. For one who has fully realized it, they grasp it before words are spoken and know it before anything is raised;

yet even this is already the second-grade view. How much more so for those who give rise to interpretations following the words, who attempt to grasp and measure with their conceptual minds, claiming attainment where there is none and claiming realization where there is none—such people are worlds apart from the gate of the Patriarchs, separated by a distance of eighty thousand miles. How could they possibly be included among those who have truly trodden the path?

Those who tread upon the secure and secret ground find the workings of the mind extinguished and the illumination of wisdom liberated. One is enlightened, and all is enlightened; one is fully realized, and all is fully realized.
Thereafter, there is not a single thing to be attained, nor does one walk alongside the thousand sages.

Such a person is fit to be a free and easy patch-robed monk who has finished the task. This matter is most simple and most easy; it is not obtained from others, nor does it transcend a single thought-moment.
Realize it directly; there is no second person, and there is no second view. The Patriarch said: "It is known clearly and constantly.
Therefore, words cannot reach it. Reaching this point, you must have a place to turn yourself around before you can succeed. Mingliao, the attendant—
We have followed one another for a year, diligent and tireless. Now, desiring to travel extensively to seek instruction, I ask for your words to serve as a companion on the road.
I write this spontaneously to show you; I offer my most sincere wishes that you persevere.
To instruct Master Cheng, the Layman:
Virtue has no fixed teacher; take what is good as your teacher. If you take what is good as your teacher, you will know whom to revere.

To exhaust principle and fully realize one's nature until reaching the mandate of destiny—this does not involve a gradual progression of stages; it must be transcended in a single thought, yet it requires ultimate realization. A monk asked Zhaozhou: "The dog..."
"Does the Son have the Buddha-dharma or not? "No. "It is not the 'no' of existence and non-existence, nor is it the 'no' of ultimate non-existence.
It is the sharp sword of the profound mystery that transcends principle; it is the wondrous Dharma that turns destiny, fortune, and calamity.

Grasp it directly from above; in that very moment, there is sudden enlightenment. Like silver mountains and iron walls—iron walls and silver mountains—the praise, blame, gain, and loss enter [into it]."
It is a gateless creation. Praise and blame, suffering and joy—none can enclose it. It does not fall into worldly sentiments, nor does it descend into saintly understandings.
It is empty yet spiritual; still yet wondrous. It leaves no trace in any place, yet it achieves perfection in every place.
When one reaches such a time, one must know there is a final word; only then is one a true great man. To realize the task of a great man is what is called being "in the world."
It is both mundane and supramundane, the most excellent of all.
I present to the scholar Zeng Xuntang the natural radiance of the fundamental ground (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Before the birth of Buddhas or the formation of sentient beings, it was perfectly interfused and boundless; yet, suddenly obscured by the veils of delusory objects, it has become turbid.
When one is submerged in the dust and toil of worldly afflictions and grasps at all sensory objects, one consequently becomes defiled by these passions.

If, in that very moment, one cannot turn the light inward to illuminate oneself, how can one transcend such myriad conditions? Regarding circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, one must neither grasp nor cling to them;

whether in speech or silence, existence or non-existence, movement or stillness, self or other—one must sever them all at once. When engaging with conditions and responding to stimuli, one should be like a whirling sword-wheel or a raging fire.
This gathering is such that not even a single hair’s breadth of trace remains. It is directly empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous.

Amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations, a single illumination brings total clarity. One proceeds straight to the state of great peace and security, where there is no longer the slightest obstruction or stagnation;
one simply experiences ease wherever one is. Ultimately, even "Buddha" does not exist—what then can be called a "sentient being"? Even "bodhi" [does not exist].
It does not stand. What do you call afflictions? In the state of solitary liberation, the bustling marketplace and the mountain forest are fundamentally no different;
bringing one to the imperial court produces no joy, and casting one into rivers and lakes produces no weariness.
This is entirely a matter of transcendent attainment—what has it to do with me? Scholar Xuntang was born into wealth and honor, yet he did not become attached to wealth and honor.

Suoluo Long built a hut at his mother’s tomb and remained there for three years; he lived on vegetables for five years, studied the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, and clarified the principles of the Buddha.
He reached a thorough mastery of the various works of the Hundred Schools of thought, yet he still felt that these were not fully understood.

Believing that the unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Patriarchs was not yet complete, he traveled far into the mountains specifically to provide a meal for the monks and invited the Master to ascend the hall, whereupon he further brought forth [this discourse].
I have received this paper and sought a word for my own practice; yet, in my unawakened state, I have inadvertently exposed my own flaws.
I humbly entreat you to urge me onward. In reply:

When one is deluded, one is deluded regarding that which is awakening; when one awakens, one awakens to that which is delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, it is like a person— [The text ends here.]
One cuts off one’s own head; once the head is severed, there is no one capable of severing it. Seeing this clearly, one directly descends into the state where there is no second thought.
As the ancient masters said: "In its brilliant clarity, there is no awakening; to have a dharma is to be deluded. When you reach this point, you cannot even stand still.
One cannot abide [in it]; if one stands, one is precarious; if one abides, one is blind. One merely emerges without following along;

one enters without returning to emptiness. Outwardly, one does not seek branches; inwardly, one does not dwell in concentration. It is necessary that the mind does not rest in the profound, the phrase does not rest in the mind, and the function does not rest in the mechanism.
Once these three are clarified, there is no need for supervision or maintenance in any place; [the truth] manifests naturally before you. All...
In whatever situation one dwells, there is no need for deliberate cultivation; clarity arises naturally.

In such a state, meeting it at every moment is not considered intimacy, and being far removed from it is not considered distance. Amidst the flow of responding to circumstances, one is not hindered by affairs; sitting upright in stillness, one is not deluded regarding principle.
Taking charge wherever one is, one encounters conditions as the very source. Emerging and withdrawing, rolling up and unrolling, one attains great sovereign freedom. Furthermore—

One must know that there is a "hole above" before one can attain it. The Grand Councilor and Minister of the Imperial Library, Yuanqiao Zhenyi, has taken an interest in the Buddha-dharma and consulted with teachers and friends, wishing to find a companion to clarify its meaning.

Although there were over a hundred monks in the mountain this summer, they were all at the stage of study and were not yet fit to approach a great layman (*dāyādhuśrin*) for dialogue. I am but a clumsy fellow.
I have written these words directly to face you. I hope you will approach them with intimacy and seek their meaning; you will surely lift your beard and laugh aloud.
This is a small Buddhist service.
On the anniversary of Master Xueyan’s passing, I offer incense and say:
"Everyone says the former master died today; they do not know that today is his birthday. What evidence is there for this?
Purple sandalwood and yellow sandalwood are burned together in one place. Words from the past are raised today; past and present are one moment, devoid of even a hair's breadth of distinction."
"Severing all ties. Great assembly, do you still see the Old Monk? He stood motionless while offering incense and said, "His countenance is present before us;
two colors, one match.
This was the incense offering on the anniversary of Zen Master Zhou’s death.
What kind of being is this? A falcon from the vast heavens; amidst ten thousand layers of clouds, it makes but a single dash.
If you can see this clearly here, then you will rise and fall together with the Patriarch, releasing and gathering together with him. If this is not yet so, who is it that has a head three feet long?
Facing one another in silence, standing alone on one foot. *Du!* (A shout)
For the interment of Chan Master Ying, stone windows and oil lamps were used. Ying, Ying—beauty as flawless as jade. He rode the donkey of Yangqi; stern and cold as frost, he was without shadow.
At such a moment, what is it like? "The man with clear eyes falls into the well."
Venerable Head Xian rises;

his skeletal form leads the monastic community. Where the mountains are high and the waters deep, the events of the Worthy Kalpa (Bhadrakalpa) exist only in the present moment. The skull-eyes are alive as the old dragon roars;
turning one’s body to look outside the gate, the crimson sun ascends the perilous peak.
The Recorded Sayings of National Preceptor Haiin (Concluded).
Epitaph.
Formerly Attendant Scholar of the Council of State, Grand Master of the Second Class, both...
Composed by Li Tí of Hedong, Commissioner for the Transport of the Capital of Zhejiang.
I came to Jiangyou in the Dinghai year of the Zhizhi era (1347) and began serving as an administrator in Yichun, where I first met the Master at Muping; we immediately became close friends.

Subsequently, when he resided at Huili, I happened to be the Magistrate of Linjiang, which allowed me the leisure to devote myself entirely to discussing the Way with him. We remained together for three years.
Our correspondence was frequent and intimate. In the year of Dingwei, while I was governing Nanjian, the Master came to Yuzhang to see me off.

Not long after, the Master also went to reside at Jianfu Monastery. Our inquiries remained constant, and he once sent me copies of the recorded sayings of the former Abbot of the Pagoda, as well as the sermons and general discourses (*pushe*) of the Master himself;
his earnest devotion was evident therein. In the spring of the year of Renzi, I departed from Quannan.

While transporting grain through the two provinces of Zhejiang, he heard that the Master had returned to Huili. On the sixteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he bathed and passed away while seated.
Alas! For twenty-six years, we had seen one another, heard one another, ascended heights together, exchanged greetings, and ultimately analyzed the principles of the Dharma.
Was this not the natural course of human feeling, as between Han Yu and Dadian, or Su Shi and Foyin? The following year, his disciples...
Xingchun submitted a description of his master’s life and requested an inscription for his stele. The Master’s surname was Yang, his given name was Zhaoru, and he styled himself Haiyin.
His family had resided in Xingan, Linjiang, for generations. He was born on the twentieth day of the twelfth month in the *bingwu* year of the Chunyou era of the Song dynasty.

As the son of a member of the Lotus Society (*lianshe*), he would chant Buddhist hymns (*fanbai*) alongside his mother, Lady Zou, as soon as he could speak. At the age of seven, he left home to study the Buddha-dharma. He resided at...
In the Incense Chamber Hall of Jianxing Temple in the prefecture, at the age of nineteen, he received the imperial edict of the Xianchun era and shaved his head to become a monk.
He first studied under the śramaṇa Zhining, and subsequently paid homage to the Patriarch Xueyan Zhenqin, from whom he attained the Dharma.
While serving as the First Seat in Jiyuntang, in the Gengchen year of the Zhizheng era, he accompanied Xueyan into the capital.
He had an audience [with the Emperor]. An imperial decree granted him a robe made of hemp. He returned and resided at Muping for ten years, and at Hyeil for nineteen years;
it was actually the *Xinmao* year of the *Shizun* era when he first arrived. This was the *Bingshen* year of the *Yuanzhen* era.
He was bestowed the title of Great Zen Master Puzhao and granted a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*. Goryeo also provided him with robes, accompanied by a golden scripture and a jade chalice.

From the western reaches of Yunnan to the eastern shores of Liaodong, Zen practitioners flocked from all quarters; yet, as the supply of simple gruel and porridge gradually failed to keep pace, his resources became strained.
At times he served as a pawn for others, tirelessly striking and brushing away [obstacles] so that the multitude remained at peace.
In the year Jǐyǒu of the Zhìdà era, the Xíng Xuānzhènyuàn court summoned the Master to serve as the abbot of Jiànfú Monastery. Jiànfú was a major monastery in Fànzhōu;

the legacy of the Tang dynasty’s Yán and the Song dynasty’s Fàn had not yet faded, and it relied upon the Master to restore its prestige. Yet the Master was already exhausted due to illness. Nevertheless, his reputation spread throughout the world, and his conduct—

He was trusted by people; they regarded the West River as being even more abundant [in offerings] for him. In the spring of last year, he returned to Huili. Disciples from the West River region actually provided a boat for him.

Upon arrival, he still preached the Dharma to the assembly despite his physical ailment. At the beginning of summer, he returned to his incense chamber and visited the places where he had frequently traveled.

He praised the longevity of the Incense Accumulation (Xiangji) Heaven, ascended Mount Yang to pay homage at the Re-appeared Stupa, and visited Cihua. Wherever he went, [he was received with reverence].
He greeted his old friends and, one night, secretly prepared his boat for departure. Upon arriving at the East Hermitage of Ruijun, his illness had already reached its terminal stage.

Xingchun further recounted that when the Master was nursing, a purple caul appeared as an auspicious sign, and a dragon emerged from within the earth. When he passed away, after a long drought, a great thunderstorm suddenly broke out.
Four days after his death, his coffin was enshrined and cremated; wherever the flying smoke and remaining embers reached, *śarīra* relics were found.
[His remains] were like millet, like foxtail millet, or like beans; his teeth and gums remained as if alive, and his prayer beads were unbroken.
His stupa now enshrines his relics within the Green Stone Garden of his native village. He lived for a total of sixty-seven years and served as a monk for forty-eight years.

The Dharma discourses, verses, and hymns he preached numbered several hundred thousand words. He ordained more than sixty individuals from the same clan, and these are those who have succeeded to his Dharma.

It is not easy to enumerate [his virtues] in full. As for the Master’s character: he was clear-sighted and quick-witted, refined and elegant, possessing wisdom and great capacity. People never saw him display joy or anger.
Having read the Five Classics but once, he could recite them from memory. His calligraphy bore an air of antiquity. Among those with whom he associated, many were of high standing and honor.

In the monastic communities today, one such as the Master can no longer be easily found. Given the Master’s life and conduct, how could there not be an inscription? The inscription reads: [The rest of the inscription follows.]
Internally he investigated the ultimate truth; externally he spread forth upright words. As the moon sets over a thousand rivers, its light shines universally at once.
His teacher’s seat was a place of high honor where monks gathered like clouds. When the provisions of gruel and rice were slightly lacking, he would either beg or pawn his belongings.
After three years at Donghu, he yearned for Xijing; he prepared a boat in advance and, with courageous resolve, withdrew to return home.
Filled with joy, I hasten here; pressing on despite my illness, I expound the Dharma. Since the robe has been transmitted, I ascend once more to the Patriarch’s stupa.
His life was extraordinary, and his passing was miraculous; the śarīra relics are abundant, leaving no doubt for those who see or hear them.
Through the accumulation of meritorious deeds, his realization of Great Enlightenment was as clear as ice melting away. I have briefly gathered these remnants to inscribe upon this joyous stone.
Epitaph composed by Zeng Deyu of Luling, Former Palace Scholar and Acting Vice-Director of the Hanlin Academy,
Knight of the Second Class, Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts, and Joint Editor of the National History.
The sages of the West, through the eye of the True Dharma, transmitted [the teaching] directly to the four and seven patriarchs, which eventually reached this eastern land.

Subsequently, it branched into five schools, among which the Linji school was the most flourishing. Toward the end of the Song dynasty, there was a master named Xueyan who dwelt at Mount Yang in Yuan;
his Dharma voice thundered like a clap of lightning, greatly reviving his lineage. His foremost disciple in receiving the Dharma was Haoyin Zhi.
He has realized the extraordinary and opened the most supreme path; the value of his Way is proclaimed in all directions, and its profound influence spreads beyond our borders.

At that time, many worthy scholars and gentlemen delighted in following him as their companion, and among them, my younger brother Xunchu was well-acquainted with him. Now that I have retired from public life to dwell in seclusion, I deeply lament my former delusions;
I am now about to follow a teacher to elucidate the primary truth (*paramārtha*), so as to cleanse away the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conditioned existence.

The Master having already entered nirvana, two years later, the Head Seat Huili, while in seclusion, presented the Master’s life and deeds to my younger brother Qiu, requesting an inscription for his stupa.
Consequently, I could not refuse and have thus composed this narrative and inscription. The Master’s name was Zhaoru; his surname was Yang.

His family was established in Xin Gan, bordering the Yangtze River. Both his parents were devoted to Buddhism; there were extraordinary signs at the time of his birth. As soon as he began to speak, he would recite Buddhist scriptures following his mother.
At the age of seven, he left the household life under the monk Zhining of the Xiangshi Monastery in Jianxing.

By nature, he was intelligent and quick-witted; his reading and recitation were fluent and proficient, and he never forgot anything after a single reading. At nineteen, he shaved his head; the following year, he received full ordination and traveled to study in various regions.

He went to attend upon Xueyan. Xueyan showed him the koan of "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature," which he could not yet resolve. Later, while traveling to Mount Nanyue in the autumn, after a rain he was crossing the Jiao River when his foot slipped;
in that sudden moment, he attained realization. Upon returning to Mount Yangshan, he devoted himself to the refinement of Chan practice.

One day, as Xueyan opened his room for instruction, the Master was about to speak when Xueyan struck him with a bamboo staff. At that moment, he attained great enlightenment. Xueyan ordered him back to the service quarters and subsequently appointed him to oversee the library. Together—
The members of the hall all yielded to him, so that he returned to his home province to attend upon his preceptor, who was elderly; he remained there for half a year.

When Chen Zhongwei of Gaoyang, an attendant official, visited him, he marveled at his conversation and composed a poem for him. He returned once more to Mount Yang, where he occupied the second seat in the assembly.
He applied himself with even greater intensity to his ascetic practices, and ten years passed.
In the year Gengchen of the Sagely Yuan era, Suian responded to an imperial summons and traveled to the capital,
where he stayed at Seongsan-sa Temple. While Suian was removing his travel pack and scratching an itch, a monk happened to be reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the lands, the practices, and the perfect enlightenment, he questioned the Master on their meaning. The Master’s responses satisfied the mind of Chak-yam, who then prostrated himself.
On the first day of the sixth month, he went to the mountain to pay his respects;

as was customary, he was granted a robe made of hemp. He returned to the mountain and occupied the position of the First Seat (Daisō). When the public nominated him to reside at Mokp’ing Monastery, there were many senior monks in residence.

Everyone was delighted and found peace in this. In the tenth year, he retired to the Puguang Hall. In the *xinmao* year, at the request of the assembly, he resided at Huili on the banks of the Jiang River.

Before a full year had passed, monks who specialized in exegesis arrived and took possession of the site; the practitioners of Chan had nowhere to settle and were forced to live in scattered dwellings while seeking food.

Like ants drawn to sweetness, they could not bear to leave. The Master exerted his efforts to restore it as a Chan center, until finally they all returned together. From then on, students flocked there like a herd of deer, and the daily provisions were abundant.

The community numbered several hundred people, yet the temple’s regular income was insufficient to sustain them. When they reached the point of having to beg and borrow to provide for their needs, and even that failed to continue, they would pawn their robes and alms bowls.

Those who were held in debt stood in rows like geese, yet the Master treated them with serene composure. In his daily life, he never had a day when the monastics and laypeople did not come to seek his counsel.

The Master was composed and humble, blending compassion with wisdom; he viewed the noble and the lowly as equals, welcoming and guiding them without weariness. Some even obtained a few words from him.
There was no one who was not satisfied. His calligraphy and ink were especially treasured by people.
